name: The Kuznets Curve
statement: The Kuznets curve hypothesises that income inequality first rises then falls as a country’s economy develops, tracing an inverted U-shape.
statementAccent: inequality first rises then falls as a country’s economy develops
meaning: Proposed by Simon Kuznets, the hypothesis describes a relationship between a country’s level of economic development and its degree of income inequality. Early in industrialisation inequality is predicted to rise, then after some threshold to fall, producing an inverted-U shape when plotted. It was originally a hypothesis about long-run structural change, not a proven universal law.
mechanism: Kuznets argued the pattern arises as workers migrate from low-income, more equal agricultural sectors into higher-income but initially unequal industrial and urban sectors, so early gains accrue disproportionately to owners and skilled workers. As the urban workforce share grows past roughly half the labour force, wages broaden and education and social policy catch up, so inequality is predicted to decline.

examples.text: Simon Kuznets presented the hypothesis in "Economic Growth and Income Inequality," American Economic Review vol. 45 (1955), based on his 1954 presidential address to the American Economic Association.

The framework was later extended to pollution: some pollutants such as sulphur dioxide and airborne lead have shown an inverted-U pattern against income as nations industrialised and then adopted cleaner technology.

Several rapidly industrialising East Asian economies in the late 20th century grew quickly while inequality fell or stayed low rather than first rising — a pattern frequently cited as contradicting the curve.

whyItMatters: The curve shaped decades of development economics, suggesting rising inequality could be an acceptable, temporary by-product of growth that would self-correct — a claim with major implications for redistribution policy.
limits: Empirically, inequality has risen rather than fallen in many advanced economies since the 1970s, contradicting the predicted downward leg. Critics argue the apparent U-shape in Kuznets’s data may reflect one-time historical circumstances — wars, the Great Depression, specific tax and labour institutions — rather than a universal law, and cases such as East Asia do not fit. Kuznets himself cautioned that his data were fragile and his claims speculative.
misreadings: It is often misreported as an established empirical law guaranteeing inequality will eventually fall with growth, when Kuznets presented it as a tentative hypothesis with explicit reservations about the thinness of the underlying data.
origin: Proposed by Belarusian-American economist Simon Kuznets in his 1954 AEA presidential address and 1955 paper "Economic Growth and Income Inequality" (American Economic Review vol. 45).
